planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring into very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; trailing ice plant roots easily from stem sections pressed directly into soil and spreads quickly to cover ground.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; trailing ice plant produces a dazzling spring display of large, glossy, daisy-like flowers in vivid purple, magenta, pink, orange, or white, packed so densely over the succulent, three-angled foliage that the plant is often completely obscured by bloom for several weeks. It spreads quickly by trailing stems that root readily at the nodes, making it one of the fastest ways to cover a dry, sunny bank or slope with color, and it is a mainstay of coastal and Mediterranean-climate xeriscape plantings. Established mats need almost no supplemental water and thrive on neglect, but they are frost-tender and can be damaged or killed by hard freezes, so gardeners at the cold edge of its range should keep rooted cuttings as insurance. Shear back after the main spring bloom to keep growth dense and encourage a tidier summer appearance.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring into very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; coppery mesemb is widely used along roadsides and highway slopes for erosion control because of its rapid, dense spread.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; coppery mesemb forms a dense, fast-spreading mat of gray-green, cylindrical succulent leaves studded with copper-orange to salmon flowers with a yellow center, opening in bright sun over a long spring to summer bloom season. Its rapid growth and deep, soil-binding root system make it one of the most widely planted groundcovers for erosion control on dry highway embankments, freeway slopes, and other large, difficult-to-irrigate sites. It tolerates poor, sandy, and saline soil with ease, needing supplemental water only to establish a new planting, after which mature mats are essentially self-sufficient on rainfall alone in mild coastal climates. Being frost-tender, it is best reserved for essentially frost-free gardens or replanted annually from cuttings where hard freezes are likely.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring into very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; rosea ice plant forms a fine-textured, low, dense mat that roots as it spreads across bare ground.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; rosea ice plant forms a fine-textured, densely branched mat of tiny, glistening, cylindrical leaves covered so thickly in pale pink to lilac-pink flowers each spring that the foliage nearly disappears beneath the bloom for several weeks. Its finer texture and lower profile compared to trailing ice plant make it especially useful for softening the edges of paths, rock walls, and gravel beds where a delicate groundcover is wanted. Extremely drought tolerant once established, it thrives on minimal water in full sun and mineral, fast-draining soil, and it spreads and roots along the ground to knit bare areas together within a season or two. Being frost-tender, protect or take cutting insurance in colder parts of its zone range, and shear lightly after bloom to maintain a tight, tidy mat.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions after last frost into well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; heartleaf ice plant tolerates more shade and moisture than most other ice plants, and roots easily from stem cuttings.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; heartleaf ice plant has distinctive small, glossy, heart-shaped succulent leaves quite different from the narrow, cylindrical foliage typical of most ice plants, and it tolerates more shade and regular moisture than its stricter desert-adapted relatives. Small, bright magenta-pink, daisy-like flowers open in sunny conditions over a long warm-season bloom, and the trailing stems root readily wherever they touch soil, quickly filling in as a groundcover, hanging basket trailer, or container spiller. It is fast-growing and easy from cuttings, making it simple to propagate extra plants for filling in bare spots or sharing. Being frost-tender, treat it as an annual or take cuttings to overwinter indoors in climates colder than its hardiness range, and pinch back leggy growth to keep plantings full and compact.

planting.note: Plant divisions or small starts in spring into very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; Red Mountain ice plant is a cold-hardy South African hardy ice plant selection valued for its intense red-orange flower color.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; Red Mountain ice plant forms a dense, low mat of small succulent leaves smothered in late spring to early summer with vivid red-orange, satiny flowers that hold their color intensity better in heat than many other hardy ice plant selections. It is part of a group of cold-hardy Delosperma species and hybrids that have expanded ice plant use well beyond the frost-free regions where tender South African species are normally limited, tolerating winters that would kill Lampranthus or Aptenia outright. Sharp drainage remains essential, since winter wet rather than cold is the main threat to this otherwise tough and drought-tolerant groundcover. Use it in rock gardens, gravel mulch beds, and dry slopes where its mat-forming habit and long bloom season provide reliable color with minimal maintenance once established.
